verdict: The Korean-specific thinking here is genuinely good where it exists: 해요 is held as the default throughout, the address problem (당신 correctly marked N/A, 저기요 / 사장님 / 기사님 / 씨·님 taught properly), the two number systems, 안 versus 못, 있다/없다/아니다, the free 반찬 and the 멸치-stock warning for vegetarians are all called the way a Korean curriculum should call them. The damage is structural rather than doctrinal. First, roughly ninety items are straight duplicates of earlier ones (김치, 반찬, 저녁, 되다, 아프다, 전부 and 사장님 each appear three times, often at conflicting tiers), which in an SRS deck means the same card front served repeatedly and about a fifth of tiers 2 and 3 spent on nothing. Second, the notes are still visibly a Hindi deck wearing Korean clothes: editorial metadata is showing in learner-facing text ("re-tiered up", "the spine slot wanted", "this slot's real work"), and a British learner is told about दादा/नाना, साला, paneer, khichdi, parson and "the Hindi meter-haggle", none of which mean anything to them. Third, and most seriously for production, there are real teaching holes a Hindi spine would never flag: no irregular-stem rule at all, so the learner meets 더워요, 매워요, 들어요, 몰라요, 써요 and 나아요 as unexplained one-offs; no -(으)ㄹ게요, no -네요 (which the deck's own notes use at 날씨 좋네요), and no way to form 합니다 though the brief asks for awareness of it; no statement that the verb comes last and that subjects are dropped, which is new information for an English speaker even though it was not for a Hindi one. Walking the day, the learner cannot say "get on the bus" (타다 and 갈아타다 are absent), cannot name the 편의점 or the 식당, cannot check in, cross a road, give a floor number, ask for a receipt, answer 드시고 가세요?, order a beer, say 잘 먹겠습니다, or ask the age question that decides which speech level everyone will use for the rest of the encounter. Two items are marked N/A when a perfectly ordinary Korean word exists (처남, 가사도우미), 사장님 is glossed as male-only when it is gender-neutral, hs-0273's note is garbled, hs-0118 wrongly says native numbers stop at twenty while hs-0748 teaches them to ninety, and hs-0721 and hs-1038 contradict each other on what 자리 있어요? asks. Fix the duplicates, strip the Hindi and the editorial voice out of the notes, and add the six grammar patterns and the day-in-the-life vocabulary above, and this becomes a genuinely strong travel-and-conversation syllabus.

items.note: 이에요 after a consonant, 예요 after a vowel: 학생이에요, 의사예요. Dictionary form 이다.
Sits straight in front of the verb: 안 가요, 안 매워요. With a 하다 verb it splits the noun off: 공부 안 해요, never 안 공부해요. 'No' as an answer is 아니요.
Also the all-purpose 'mm-hm' of a phone call. 예 is the stiffer variant.
The humble 'I' you use with everyone in 해요 speech. 제가 as subject, 제 as 'my'. 나/내 is banmal.
Korean sidesteps 'you': address people by title (선생님, 사장님, 기사님) or drop the subject entirely.
뭐예요? 'what is it?'. 무엇 is the written form.
One verb for existence and possession: 시간 있어요? 'have you got a minute?', 여기 있어요 'it's here'.
The negative copula, 아니다. Also a modest 'not at all' when thanked.
Before a noun it's just 이: 이 사람. Full form 이것.

items.en: that one (by you) / that one over there
items.note: Korean splits 'that' in two: 그 = near the listener or already mentioned, 저 = away from both of you.
제 가방 is 저의 contracted. Spoken Korean often just stacks the nouns: 친구 집 'my friend's place'.

items.en: in; at; to (a place or a time)
items.note: 서울에 가요, 세 시에 만나요, 집에 있어요. Static location and destination.
을 after a consonant, 를 after a vowel: 밥을 먹어요, 커피를 마셔요. Dropped constantly in speech.
버스로 가요 'by bus', 오른쪽으로 'to the right'. 'From a place' is 에서, 'from a time' is 부터.
Where an action happens – 식당에서 먹어요 – and where you came from: 영국에서 왔어요. Contrast with 에, which is for being somewhere.
Joins nouns: 김치하고 밥. 랑 casual, 와/과 written, 그리고 links whole sentences.
저는 영국 사람이에요. Sets what the sentence is about and quietly contrasts. 은 after a consonant, 는 after a vowel.
Koreans say 'our' where English says 'my': 우리 집, 우리 엄마. Humble form 저희.
Close friends, children and juniors only. 네가 as subject, said 'niga' so it isn't heard as 내가.
The banmal answer to 네. Using it upwards is rude – worth recognising more than saying.

items.en: the politeness tag on the end of a sentence
items.note: Add 요 and you're polite; strip it and you're in banmal. It even props up bare words: 저요? 여기요, 조금만요.
Covers morning, afternoon and evening. Said with a small nod.

items.en: it's fine; that's alright; no thanks
items.note: Accepts, reassures and politely refuses, depending on tone. 괜찮아요? = 'are you alright?'
'Oh, I see' is 아, 그래요? or 그렇구나.
Pushes out 은/는 and 이/가 rather than stacking: 저도요 'me too'.
해요. Turns nouns into verbs wholesale: 공부하다, 전화하다, 사랑하다.

items.en: to become; to work out; to be OK
items.note: 돼요. 안 돼요 is the everyday 'no, that's not on'; 다 됐어요 'it's all done'.
가요.
와요.

items.en: present tense, polite: 가요 = I go / I'm going
items.note: Stems with ㅏ or ㅗ take 아요 (가요, 좋아요), everything else takes 어요 (먹어요, 마셔요), 하다 becomes 해요. This one form is your default for the whole trip.
제 이름, 제 가방, 제 거예요 'it's mine'. Casual 내.
저한테 주세요. Written 저에게, casual 나한테. For 'I like / I need', Korean makes you the topic instead: 저는 …이 좋아요.
친구한테 말했어요. 에게 in writing, 께 when the person outranks you: 선생님께.
누구예요? As subject it contracts: 누가 왔어요?
화장실 어디예요? 어디 가세요?
On its own, 왜요? = 'why, what's up?'
어떻게 가요? 'how do I get there?'
몇 시예요?, 몇 명이요?, 몇 개요? Price is a different word, 얼마.
여기요! also flags down a server.
Same three-way split as 이/그/저.
바로 갈게요 'I'll come straight over', 바로 앞이에요 'it's right in front of you'.
Two separate words, and neither doubles for the other. 오늘 밤 = tonight, 어젯밤 = last night.
또 오세요 'do come again'. 'Then, in that case' is 그럼.
Strictly 'excessively', but in speech it's the everyday 'very': 너무 맛있어요. 아주 and 정말 also work.
Squeezed to 좀 in speech, where it doubles as the politeness softener.
더 주세요 'a bit more, please'; 조금 더.
덜 맵게 해 주세요 'make it less spicy'.
Waves off a top-up or an offer. Sharpened by tone into 'that'll do', so keep it light.
다 먹었어요 'I've eaten the lot'. 모두 is the fuller word.
어떤 거요? 'which one?'; 어떤 사람이에요? 'what's he like?'
아무거나 주세요 'anything's fine'; 아무도 없어요 'there's nobody in'.
한국 사람 'a Korean'. 사람들 pluralises when it matters.
한국말 'the Korean language'; 말이 안 돼요 'that makes no sense'.
일해요 'I work'; 무슨 일이에요? 'what's up?' Same syllable as Sino 'one' and 'day'.
Tacked onto shop types: 고깃집 'meat restaurant', 술집 'pub'.
Honorific 성함 shows up on forms and in formal questions.
Free and self-service in Korean restaurants; 물 좀 주세요 if you can't spot the jug.
Coffee is what you get offered and what you meet over; the café is the default meeting place. 차 = tea, 녹차 green tea.
Means the grain and the meal at once: 밥 먹었어요? 'have you eaten?'. 식사 is the formal word.
시간 있어요? 'have you got time?' Also counts hours: 두 시간 'two hours'.
거 is the spoken form: 이거, 그거, 제 거.
데 is the everyday spoken variant: 좋은 데 알아요 'I know a good place'.
주세요 'please give me' is the single most useful thing you can say in Korea. Honorific 드리다 when you give upwards.

items.en: to receive; to take (what's handed over)
items.note: 받아요. Taking something away is 가져가다.

items.en: to see; to watch; to look
items.note: 봐요. 좀 볼게요 'just having a look' in a shop.
들어요 – the ㄷ turns into ㄹ before a vowel.
말해요. Korean uses this one verb where English splits 'speak' and 'say'.

items.en: to talk; to tell someone about something
items.note: 얘기해요; full form 이야기하다.
만나요. 만나서 반갑습니다 'pleased to meet you'.
알아요. The ㄹ drops before certain endings: 아세요? 'do you know?'
몰라요. Korean gives 'not knowing' its own verb – never 안 알아요.
In speech 알겠어요 / 모르겠어요 do most of this job.
살아요. 서울에 살아요 'I live in Seoul'.
가고 싶어요 'I'd like to go', 먹고 싶어요. For wanting a thing, use …이/가 필요해요 or just …주세요.
마셔요. Honorific 드시다 covers eating and drinking alike.
걸어요 – ㄷ to ㄹ again. 걸어서 가요 'let's walk it'.
만들어요.
놓아요/놔요. 두다 is 'to leave something somewhere'.

items.en: commands and requests at three politeness levels
items.note: 앉으세요 is your everyday polite request; 앉아 is banmal; 앉으십시오 belongs to signs and announcements. Add 주세요 to ask a favour: 도와주세요.

items.en: right then; come on; off we go
items.note: The get-moving opener: 자, 갈까요? 자, 드세요.
어서 오세요 is what shops and restaurants call out as you walk in.
여기 앉으세요, with a hand gesture at the seat.
Hand things over with two hands, or with your left hand touching your right forearm.
말씀 is the honorific word for someone else's speech.
The default apology to strangers and for anything that matters. 죄송해요 is a shade softer.
For friends and small mishaps. 미안해 in banmal. To an older stranger, use 죄송합니다 instead.

items.en: just; a bit – the softener in every request
items.note: 물 좀 주세요, 이것 좀 보여 주세요. Korean has no standalone word for 'please': 좀 plus -주세요 carries it.

items.en: not at all; don't mention it
items.note: Reply to thanks. 아니에요 and 괜찮아요 do the same job and are heard more.
아뇨 in quick speech. Note the mismatch with English: answering 안 가요? with 네 means 'right, I'm not going'.
Koreans don't ask 'how are you?' at every meeting – 안녕하세요 already covers it. Save this for someone you haven't seen in a while.
Hang 는요? off the person's name: 민수 씨는요? Never 당신은요?
Point at the menu and say it – the workhorse question of a food trip.
저는 앤이에요. 제 이름은 …예요 is the fuller version.
Politer: 성함이 어떻게 되세요? – note that neither says 'your'.
-아/어야 돼요 is the general 'have to': 지금 가야 돼요.
The spoken workhorse, from 그런데. 하지만 belongs to writing.
Between nouns, use 나/이나 instead: 커피나 차.
Korean puts the reason first and glues it on: 늦어서 죄송해요 'sorry I'm late'. 왜냐하면 is stiff and rare in speech.
All-purpose: surprise, sympathy, and the noise Koreans make standing up.
Korean runs two number systems. Native numbers count things, people and hours – 한 개, 한 명, 한 시. Sino numbers (일, 이, 삼 …) do money, dates, minutes and phone numbers.
두 개, 두 명이요 'a table for two', 두 시. Sino form 이.
세 개, 세 시. Sino form 삼.
네 개, 네 시. Sino form 사 – which sounds like the word for death, so some lifts label the 4th floor F.
Sino form 오.
Sino form 육.
Sino form 칠.
Sino form 팔. The ㅂ is silent.
Sino form 구.
Sino form 십. The native set keeps going for ages and for counting things: 스물, 서른, 마흔 … 아흔.
어머니 is the formal word; 어머님 when speaking to or about someone else's mother.
아버지 formal, 아버님 for someone else's father.

items.en: older brother – 형 if you're male, 오빠 if you're female
items.note: Korean has no single word for 'brother': younger brother is 남동생, and which word you use depends on your own sex.

items.en: older sister – 누나 if you're male, 언니 if you're female
items.note: Younger sister is 여동생. These four terms are also used for close non-relatives slightly older than you.

items.en: auntie – what you call the woman running a restaurant
items.note: Literally 'mum's sister'. 이모님! is how regulars call the server over; warmer than 저기요.

items.en: boss – how you address any shop or restaurant owner
items.note: Safe and slightly flattering for whoever is behind the counter, man or woman – 사장님 carries no gender. 기사님 for a driver, 선생님 when you're unsure.
A real greeting in Korean too, with the same warmth as in Hindi. 식사하셨어요? is the polite version for older people.
Reliably produces delight and then a torrent of fast Korean.
A rising 네? on its own does the same job.
알겠습니다 is the crisp version staff use.

items.en: I don't understand; I'm not sure
items.note: The 잘 softens it – a bare 몰라요 can land as blunt.

items.en: how do you say this in Korean?

items.note: 한국말 is the everyday spoken word for it.
The benefactive: 도와주세요 'help me', 사 주세요 'buy it for me', 깎아 주세요 'knock a bit off'. Attach it to any verb and a demand becomes a request.
친구하고 같이 갔어요. 랑 같이 in casual speech.
이 근처에 편의점 있어요? 'is there a shop near here?'
갈 수 있어요 'I can go'. The quick spoken negative is 못: 못 가요 'I can't go'.
빨리빨리 is close to a national motto.
Native numbers with 시, Sino numbers with 분: 두 시 삼십 분 'half two'.
Strictly someone your own age – Koreans won't call a person five years older 친구.
아줌마 is the casual clip, and can sting if she thinks she's too young for it.
남자 친구 = boyfriend. 소년 'boy' is literary.
여자 친구 = girlfriend.
Korean rarely labels a stranger 'the man' or 'the woman' – it says 이분, 저분 'this/that gentleman or lady'. 몇 분이세요? 'how many in your party?'
두 명이요 'two of us' at a restaurant door. 분 is its polite twin.
데려오다 for bringing a person along.
열어요. 몇 시에 열어요? 'what time do you open?'
닫아요. 문 닫았어요 'they're shut'. Switching something off is 끄다.
휴대폰 is the tidier word; just 폰 in speech. 카톡 (KakaoTalk) is how everyone actually messages.
Never used face to face.
전화해요. 전화 = a phone call.
통화 중이에요 'the line's busy / he's on a call'.
It lands on the table at every single meal and turns up in dozens of dish names: 김치찌개, 김치전, 김치볶음밥.
면 in dish names: 라면, 냉면, 짜장면. Uncooked rice is 쌀.

items.en: soup – the bowl that comes with the rice
items.note: 찌개 is the thicker, spicier stew: 김치찌개, 된장찌개.
The free little plates that arrive with every meal. 반찬 더 주세요 gets refills, also free.
매워요. 안 맵게 해 주세요 'not spicy, please' – worth having ready on day one.
Meals are 아침 (breakfast), 점심 (lunch), 저녁 (dinner).
드시다 is the honorific 'eat'; 많이 드세요 'tuck in'.
맛없어요 is 'it's not nice' – keep that one to yourself.
Same syllable as 차 'tea'; context does the work. 택시 for a taxi.
Everywhere in Korean life: 노래방 karaoke room, 찜질방 sauna, PC방 internet café.
Prices are read in units of 만 (10,000): 만 원 is roughly £6.
전부 얼마예요? 'how much altogether?'
Also 'hold that thought' and 'stop right there'.
커요. 더 큰 거 있어요? 'have you got a bigger one?'
작아요. Careful with 적다 'to be few', which sounds close.
Almost always paired with -(으)ㄹ 거예요: 아마 올 거예요.
좋아해요 'I like it' versus 좋아요 'it's nice' – the second is about the thing, the first about you.

items.en: by any chance; if I may ask
items.note: Opens a question politely: 혹시 영어 하세요?
대한민국 is the official name; 한국 on its own means the South.
캐리어 for a wheeled suitcase.

items.en: three verbs where English has one 'be'
items.note: A이에요 = A is (identity). 있어요 = there is / I have. 없어요 = there isn't / I haven't. Negative identity is its own verb again: 아니에요.
그래 in banmal. With a rising tone, 그래요? = 'oh really?'
The everyday default – shops, taxis, strangers. A small bow of the head goes with it.
What the host or server says. The guest's line is 잘 먹겠습니다 before eating, 잘 먹었습니다 after.
Point and say it. Swap in any number: 두 개 주세요.
마음에 들어요 – used of something you've just been shown or given.
잘 모르겠어요 is the softer, more polite version.
혹시 영어 하세요? is softer still.
어느 나라 사람이에요? is the plainer version.
영국 사람이에요 'I'm British'. Expect 어! 영국! and a comment about football.
Or drop the particle: 지하철역 어디예요?
On the phone: 저 앤인데요.
Also what you say squeezing past someone on a packed underground.
Say 안녕히 계세요 if you're the one walking out. Friends just get 잘 가요.
건강하세요 'keep well' is the version for older people.
The standard Korean invitation to sit and talk.
애 in speech; 아기 for a baby.
돼지고기 pork, 소고기 beef, 닭고기 chicken. 고기 빼 주세요 'no meat, please'.
해요 is your default everywhere as a visitor. 합니다 for announcements, service staff and first formal meetings. 반말 (just drop the 요) only downwards or with close friends – never assume your way into it.
Warmer and less formal than 감사합니다; 고마워 in banmal.
이게 = 이것이 with the subject particle. Dropping it gives 이거 뭐예요?, which is what people actually say.
다시 한번 'once more'.
From -지요. 맛있죠? 'lovely, isn't it?'; 그렇죠 'exactly'.
Sometimes met with an amused 'it's not spicy' as the sweat starts.
도움이 필요해요 'I need some help'.
The formal word. You'd say 엄마 at home and 어머님 to someone else's mother.

items.en: respect tags on names and titles
items.note: 민수 씨 (first name + 씨, for peers), 선생님·사장님·기사님 (님 on a job title). Never 씨 on a surname alone, and never on someone clearly senior to you.
배고파요. The opposite is 배부르다 'to be full'.
Possession is just 있어요: 표 있어요? 'have you got the tickets?'

items.en: there isn't; I haven't got any
items.note: Its own verb, not a negated 있어요. 시간 없어요 'I've no time'.
The pointing-at-the-menu line. 이걸로 할게요 'I'll go with this one'.
Banmal only – friends and juniors. Rude in every other direction. To flag down a stranger, use 저기요.
Turns a clause into a noun: 한국어 배우는 게 재미있어요 'learning Korean is fun'.
Spoken squeeze of 그렇죠 – a nudge for agreement.
밥 먹고 있어요 'I'm eating'. Plain 해요 already covers most English -ing, so save this for things happening at this moment.
학생이었어요 'I was a student', 의사였어요, 있었어요 / 없었어요.
Korean has no everyday 'he' or 'she'. Repeat the name, or say 그 사람 (plain) / 그분 (polite). 그 사람 거 = 'his', 'hers'.
저희 가게, 저희 회사 – what staff say to customers and juniors to elders. 우리 is the neutral one.

items.en: how is it?; what do you reckon?
items.note: 이거 어때요? Past tense 어땠어요? 'how was it?'
어느 나라 사람이에요? 어느 거요?
Counting days uses Sino 일: 3일 'three days'. Weekdays end in 요일: 월요일 Monday.

items.en: to let someone know; to tell
items.note: 알려주세요 'do let me know'.
물어봐요. 뭐 좀 물어볼게요 'can I ask you something?' – a good way to open with a stranger.
얼마나 걸려요? 'how long does it take?' – essential on any journey.
자요. Honorific 주무시다: 안녕히 주무세요 'good night'.
앉아요.

items.en: to get up; to stand up
items.note: 일어나요.
가지 마세요 'don't go', 걱정하지 마세요 'don't worry'.
Stick it after any noun and you have a polite request. The one phrase to learn before you land.
For servers, shop staff and strangers alike. 여기요! works in restaurants too.
The formal register of 고마워요; interchangeable with 감사합니다 in practice.
For someone you know, not a greeting for strangers.
김치 좋아해요. To decline without offence: 별로예요 'it's not really for me'.
시간 있으면 'if you've got time', 도착하면 'when I arrive'.
뜻 = meaning. The 'I mean…' filler is 그니까 / 그러니까.
이거만 주세요 'just this one'; 조금만요 'only a little'.
제 거예요 'it's mine'; 누구 거예요? 'whose is this?'

items.en: adjectives take a special form in front of a noun
items.note: 좋다 → 좋은 사람 'a good person', but 사람이 좋아요 'the person is nice'. Korean adjectives are verbs, so there's no gender or number to agree with.

items.en: the honorific infix for the person you're speaking about
items.note: Hidden inside 하세요, 가세요, 앉으세요. Special forms: 드시다 (eat/drink), 계시다 (be), 주무시다 (sleep), 말씀하시다 (speak). Never use it about yourself.
다음에 또 뵐게요 is the politer version.
Said warmly to older people on parting.

와이프 in casual speech; 집사람 is old-fashioned and a bit loaded.

배워요. 가르치다 = to teach.
사요. 제가 살게요 'my treat' – Koreans fight over this.
읽어요. 공부하다 is 'to study'.

items.en: to write; to use; to wear (glasses, a hat)

items.en: to try …-ing; to give it a go

몇 시에 시작해요?
끝났어요 'it's finished'.
잊어버렸어요 is the plainer 'I forgot'.

길 좀 물을게요 'may I ask for directions?'

싸요.

오래됐어요. 옛날 = the old days. For people, 나이가 많다.
뜨거워요 – said constantly as stone bowls arrive. Hot weather is 덥다.
차가워요. Cold weather is 춥다.

items.en: to break down; to be out of order
items.note: 고장 났어요 – on the sign taped to the lift.

items.en: to be right; to be correct
items.note: 맞아요 'that's right'; 맞아요? 'is that right?'

items.en: to feel good; to be in a good mood
items.note: 기분 좋아요. 행복해요 is 'happy' in the big, life-scale sense.
깨끗해요.
준비됐어요?
중요해요. 'It's needed' is 필요해요.
꼭 가 보세요 'you really must go'; 꼭이요! 'promise!'
당연하죠 is the more emphatic 'obviously'.
진짜 also works as 'really, very': 진짜 맛있어요. 정말 is its tidier twin.
많이 드세요 'do help yourself'. 꽤 is 'quite'.

items.en: how was it?; did you like it?

items.en: are you unwell?; where does it hurt?

아파요. 머리 아파요 'headache', 배 아파요 'stomach ache' – the body part goes first.

items.en: to rest; to take a break
items.note: 쉬어요. 푹 쉬세요 'get some proper rest'.
날씨 좋네요 'lovely day' – the standard opener.
더워요. 여름 = summer, and a Korean one is punishing.

회사원 = office worker, the default answer to 'what do you do?'

items.en: the countryside; back home in the sticks
items.note: Where people go for 추석 and 설날.
어느 나라 사람이에요? 'what country are you from?'
여행 = a trip; 휴일 = a public holiday.
사진 찍어 주시겠어요? 'could you take a photo for us?'
입다 = to wear (clothes); shoes get 신다 and hats 쓰다.
Written 네 but said 니, to keep it clear of 내 'my' and 네 'yes'.

items.en: that gentleman; that lady (polite third person)
items.note: 그분 거 = 'theirs'; 그분들 plural. The respectful step up from 그 사람.
그분께 when the person outranks you.
갈 때 'when you go', 어릴 때 'when I was little'.
그래서 못 갔어요. 그럼 is 'in that case', 그러니까 'so, what I mean is'.
가방 안에 'in the bag'. Same spelling as 안 'not' – position tells them apart.

책상 위에 'on the desk'.

items.en: grandparents split by side: 친- for dad's parents, 외- for mum's

attaches directly: 세 시쯤, 만 원쯤
다음 주, 다음 역 – you'll hear 다음 역 on every train
지난주, 지난달

items.en: I'm going to be a bit late
items.note: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 is the standard hedge; saying things flat sounds abrupt
이 근처에 … 있어요? = is there a … round here?
unrelated middle-aged men are 아저씨, never 삼촌

items.en: uncle and aunt terms encode which parent's sibling it is: 고모 father's sister, 이모 mother's sister
items.note: 이모 doubles as the friendly word for the woman running a small restaurant – you will hear it constantly
이웃 is the formal/collective word

items.en: words of blessing from an elder
items.note: exchanged at New Year; the physical version is 세배 (the deep bow), rewarded with 세뱃돈
생신 is the honorific of 생일 – used for grandparents, parents-in-law and bosses
a music or street festival is 축제, a different word
the other big one is 추석 (autumn harvest festival) – both shut the country down for days
the family ritual at 명절 and death anniversaries
신선해요
감기 걸렸어요 = I've caught a cold
one word for both – 병원 가요 usually just means going to the doctor
화났어요
extremely common – the warm response to any near-miss

items.en: to look round, have a wander
items.note: 그냥 구경하는 거예요 = I'm just browsing
놀러 가요 = let's go out somewhere – used by adults, not just children
여기서 내려 주세요
전화 받다 – Korean 'receives' a call rather than picking it up

items.en: to call over; to order up
items.note: 택시 불러 주세요 = call me a taxi
전화 걸다 = to make a call
Korean picks a different verb per item: shoes 신다, hats and glasses 쓰다, a bag 메다, a watch 차다
타다 = to get on. 다음 역에서 내려요
also 'to withdraw' cash: 돈 찾다
literally 'go on in' – said TO the other person, the standard Korean sign-off
The big live spectator sport, with its own chants and stadium beer. 축구 is the one people will bring up with a Brit.
편하게 하세요 = make yourself at home
조심히 가세요 = mind how you go – said at nearly every goodbye
달라요. 따로 = separately (따로 주세요 = serve/bill them separately)
비었어요; 자리 있어요? = is this seat free?
softens bad news or a refusal
이렇게 해 주세요 = do it like this
Cards and phone payments dominate, so change rarely comes up at all.
rare in Korea; more likely a blown bulb than a power cut
바람이 불어요 = it's windy
cheap and metered; hail one or use the Kakao T app
attaches to a verb stem. For wanting a THING, Korean uses 주세요 or 필요해요, not this
세 시 반 = half past three; 한 시간 반 = an hour and a half
the 합니다-level greeting – announcements, officials, a first meeting with someone senior. 안녕하세요 is the everyday default
늦게 왔어요 = came late

items.en: could you drive a bit slower

items.note: 차가 막혀요 = the traffic's bad; 교통카드 = the travel card you tap on every bus and train
the expected text after any journey
announcements say O번 승강장; 플랫폼 is also understood
signs say 영업 중
you usually pay at the till on the way out: 계산할게요
항공편 on tickets and boards
약국 = pharmacy, marked with a green cross
기침이 나요

items.word: 스물 / 서른 / 마흔 / 쉰 / 예순 / 일흔 / 여든 / 아흔
items.roman: seumul / seoreun / maheun / swin / yesun / ilheun / yeodeun / aheun
items.en: the native number tens, learned row by row
items.note: Korean's real number hurdle is not 21–99 (Sino 이십일, 삼십이… is perfectly regular) but the SECOND set: native numbers, used for hours, ages and counting things. 스물 shortens to 스무 before a counter
one ending, no matching 'then' word needed

items.en: comparative and superlative: 이게 저것보다 더 좋아요, 제일 좋아요
items.note: the adjective never changes shape, exactly as in Hindi. 가장 is the formal twin of 제일
no word for 'quarter' – 세 시 십오 분 = quarter past three
also 현금인출기; every convenience store has one
예약했어요 = I have a booking
most of the good restaurants are down one
112 for police, 119 for fire and ambulance
worn at 명절 and weddings; rental shops near the palaces get you in free
Shoes come off in homes, guesthouses, temples and floor-seating restaurants, so your socks are on show. Pack a decent pair.
the verb is 신다, not 입다

items.en: shoes off before you go in
items.note: applies in homes, guesthouses, temples and any floor-seating restaurant
the 설날 greeting, said to everyone; 추석 잘 보내세요 for the autumn holiday
the standard parting blessing to older people
토할 것 같아요 = I feel sick
땅콩 알레르기 있어요 = I'm allergic to peanuts
메뉴판 주세요 = could I see the menu

items.en: can I take this away, please
items.note: Say '포장이요' at the counter; 여기서 먹을게요 = eating in.
KakaoTalk is the WhatsApp of Korea; 카톡 is the everyday clipping.
사진 좀 찍어 주세요 = could you take a photo; 찍어 드릴까요? = shall I take one for you?
폰이 꺼졌어요 = my phone died.
All-purpose sigh of dismay, sympathy or effort; you'll hear it constantly.
What staff call after you as you leave a shop.
혼자 왔어요 = I'm on my own; 혼밥 (eating alone) and 혼술 (drinking alone) are everyday words.

items.en: excuse me (calling staff or a stranger)
items.note: The service-address workhorse. 여기요 is the shout for a waiter; Korean has no sir/madam equivalent.
Honorific of 그 사람; plural 그분들. Korean prefers names or titles over third-person pronouns.
Korean splits by direction: 돌아가다 (go back there) vs 돌아오다 (come back here).
Rarely needed: plain 했어요 already covers most English past perfect.
-(으)ㄹ까요? makes any suggestion: 먹을까요? 볼까요?
Note the subject particle, not an object: 시간이 필요해요.
여행 왔어요 = I'm here on holiday; 출장 = business trip.
카드 돼요? = do you take card? Korea is near-cashless.
다음에 또 와요 = come again next time.
한국은 처음이에요 = it's my first time in Korea.
Place words follow the noun: 편의점 뒤에.
Also 밖에 + negative = only: 이것밖에 없어요 (there's only this).
설탕 없이 = without sugar; for food orders 빼고 (leaving out) is more natural: 고수 빼고요.
한국 사람처럼 = like a Korean. 같이 works the same way.
After a noun. After a verb use -아/어서.
The standard reply to 잘 지내요? when things are just okay.
Spoken Korean usually just uses 어디: 어디 갔어요? For 'anywhere', see 아무 데나.
Also what you say through the door.
소리 좀 줄여 주세요 = turn it down a bit.
크게 말해 주세요 = please speak up. Adverbs from adjectives: 크다 to 크게.
Lives in 재미있어요 (it's fun/interesting) and 재미없어요.
시작하다 = to start; 언제 시작해요?
마음에 들어요 = I like it (it suits my heart), the standard way to say you like a thing.
Native numbers count things, people and hours; before a counter it shortens to 스물한 개, 스물한 살.
Sino numbers do money, minutes, dates, floors and phone numbers. Learn both sets in parallel.
시간 있어요? = have you got time? Also counts hours: 두 시간 = two hours.
Hours take native numbers (한, 두, 세), 반 = half.
Minutes take Sino numbers, so the two systems meet inside one clock time.
반 시간 exists but 삼십 분 is what people say.
Spoken alternative: 십 분 뒤에.
Korean marks the part of day before the hour: 아침/오후/저녁/밤 + time.
며칠 asks the day of the month; 무슨 요일이에요? asks the weekday.
Weekdays are element + 요일: moon, fire, water, wood, metal, earth, sun.
불금 ('fiery Friday') is the going-out slang.
The -님 is built in; you say 부모님 even about your own parents.
Korean uses the past tense for the state; 결혼했어요? is standard small talk. 싱글이에요 = single.
Also 작은어머니. Extended kin is low priority for a traveller.
외- prefixes everything on the mother's side: 외삼촌, 외할머니.
Re-tiered up: 이모 doubles as the warm way to address a woman running a restaurant.
Literally 'four degrees'; 육촌 = second cousin.
A wife's parents are 장인/장모 to her husband. Korean names in-laws from the speaker's side.
Wife's family home is 처가.

items.en: brother-in-law (older sister's husband, said by a woman)
items.note: A man calls the same person 매형. The term depends on the speaker's own gender.
An ordinary word, just rare for a visitor: 처남 is your wife's brother. A woman calls her husband's younger brother 시동생.

items.en: kin prefixes: husband's side, wife's side, mother's side
items.note: 시어머니 (husband's mother), 처남 (wife's brother), 외할머니 (mother's mother). Korea's live version of this rule is gender-of-speaker sibling terms: 형/오빠, 누나/언니.
친한 사이예요 = we're close. Also means the physical gap between two things.
Literally 'mouths to feed'; 우리 식구 is warmer than 가족.
여성 is the formal/written one, 남자 is the male counterpart.
Korean addresses people by title + 님, never by a generic 'sir': 선생님, 기사님, 사장님.
아줌마 is the casual clip and can offend; 아저씨 is the male equivalent.

items.en: polite warm address to a woman serving you
items.note: Standard in restaurants; 사장님 works everywhere if you're unsure.
Never to a stranger or anyone older. In practice Koreans use names and titles instead of 'you'.

items.en: how many children do you have?
items.note: 명 is the counter for people.
얼음 빼 주세요 = no ice, please. Cafes default to iced (아이스).
저녁 먹었어요? is a friendly check-in as much as a question about food, and 'evening' and 'dinner' are the same word.
The everyday cheap staple; 김밥천국 shops are on every corner.
Spicy by default. 라멘 is the Japanese kind, a different dish.
군만두 fried, 찐만두 steamed.
What Koreans eat when ill or badly hung-over; 죽 shops sell it by the tub near every hospital.
You mix it yourself; add 고추장 to taste.
Re-tiered to day one: it comes with every meal and appears in dozens of dish names.
Ordered by portions: 삼겹살 이 인분요. 불고기 is the sweet marinated beef alternative.
찌개 = thick stew; the other two you'll see everywhere are 된장찌개 and 순두부찌개.
파전 (spring onion), 김치전. The rainy-day food, eaten with 막걸리.
The little free dishes that come with every meal; refills are free, just ask 반찬 좀 더 주세요.
Salted sheets eaten with rice, sold everywhere as a snack.
쌈 = wrapping a piece of grilled meat in a leaf; the raw-leaf plate that arrives with barbecue.
The default savoury street snack; sold with 순대 and 튀김.
청양고추 is the seriously hot one.
Often served raw to grill alongside meat.
The cabbage kimchi is made from; 양배추 is the round European cabbage.
A stock side dish and the base of 콩나물국, the hangover soup.
The everyday aromatic. Coriander (고수) is rare in Korean food, unlike in Hindi cooking.
The winter fruit, sold by the box; 오렌지 is the imported orange.
The signature finishing flavour, drizzled on at the end.
The defining seasoning; 된장 is the soybean paste, 쌈장 the dipping mix.
고춧가루 = chilli powder, 소금 = salt.
The national drink, and the social ritual you'll be pulled into. 맥주 = beer, 소맥 = the two mixed.
The free tea-water on the table; 물은 셀프 means help yourself to water.
False friend: it is clear fizzy lemonade, never alcoholic cider. 콜라 = cola.
셔요 in 해요 form.
The nice kind of heat, unlike flat 맵다. 짜다 = salty, 달다 = sweet.
The 합니다 register you hear from staff and on TV; your everyday form stays 맛있어요.
무슨 맛이에요? = what does it taste of / which flavour is it?
덜 익었어요. Raw fish is 회 and is deliberate, not undercooked.
In practice say 고기 안 먹어요 (I don't eat meat) and check for 멸치/젓갈 stock, which is in almost everything.
끓이다 = to boil up (soup, ramyeon), 굽다 = to grill.
Meat at the table is cut with 가위, scissors.
The verb inside 비빔밥; 섞다 is the general 'mix'.
To urge a guest to eat you say 많이 드세요, not this verb.

items.en: how many portions would you like?
items.note: 인분 = portions per person; meat and stews are ordered this way, minimum two.
식사하세요 is the call to come to the table.

items.en: shall I heat it up for you?
items.note: Asked at every convenience store; answer 네, 데워 주세요.
Every restaurant has a 정수기 and self-serve cups; tap water is drinkable but nobody drinks it.
Korean ones are flat metal. 수저 = the spoon-and-chopsticks set.
Rice and soup are eaten with the spoon, not the chopsticks.
The one appliance in every Korean kitchen; it cooks the rice and keeps it warm all day.
반찬통 = side-dish tub.
In flat listings you'll see 방 (room) counted instead: 투룸 = two rooms.
천장 = the ceiling inside.
Where most Koreans live. 원룸 = studio flat, 고시원 = tiny cheap room.
Homes are floor-heated (온돌), so people sit and sleep on the 바닥.
The sunken bit inside the front door; shoes never go past it.
Korean doors take a 비밀번호 (code) rather than a key.
Covers both the quilt and the whole floor-bedding set.
Laid on the heated floor; 시트 is a bed sheet.
Korean summers are full of them; 모기약 = repellent.
빗자루 is a broom, but the hoover is the everyday tool.
텀블러 = reusable cup, and cafes discount you for bringing one.
치약 = toothpaste. Many Koreans brush at work after lunch.
Sorting is compulsory: 음식물 (food), 재활용 (recycling), 일반 (general).
Street bins are scarce, so people carry rubbish home.
청소하다 = to clean.
Used of weather and skin; 마르다 is what a towel does.
젖었어요 = it's wet.
빨래 = laundry, 세탁소 = the dry cleaner's.
보조배터리 = power bank; cafes and buses have chargers everywhere.
From 'concent', not English 'consent'. Korea uses 220V round two-pin. 스위치 = switch.
끄다 = to turn off. Used for lights, AC, phone, telly.
고장 났어요 = it's broken. 깨지다 = to smash.

items.en: could you put the heating on
items.note: The boiler runs both the underfloor heating and the hot water; 온수 = hot water setting.

items.en: did you turn the gas off?
items.note: Gas is 잠그다 (shut off), not 끄다.
One word for both; 머리카락 is a single strand of hair. 머리 아파요 = I've got a headache.
코가 막혔어요 = my nose is blocked.
이가 아파요; 치과 = dentist. 치아 is the polite/clinical word.
The emotional heart is 마음.
허리가 아파요 is one of the most common complaints you'll hear.
피가 나요 = it's bleeding.
정신없어요 = I'm all over the place. For 'clever' Koreans say 머리가 좋다.
숨이 차요 = I'm out of breath.
멀미 = travel sickness.

items.en: to have no energy, feel weak
items.note: 기운이 없어요. 약하다 describes a weak thing, not a poorly person.
Covers physical discomfort and social awkwardness alike.
아파요. One word covers pain and illness; 어디 아파요? = what's wrong?
Green cross sign; pharmacists speak some English in cities.
Past tense for a present state, like 결혼했어요.
Point as you say it; the most useful sentence in a Korean clinic.
What the doctor asks you, in the 세요 honorific.
부터 = from, 까지 = until.
Native day-words: 하루, 이틀, 사흘.

items.en: I think I'm going to be sick

items.note: Back it up with 못 먹어요 (I can't eat it); allergy labelling is patchy.
낫다 (to get better) is irregular: 나아요, 나았어요.
푹 = thoroughly; the standard thing to say to someone unwell.
병원 covers any clinic, so 'go to hospital' is said for a sore throat too.
Medicine is 'eaten' in Korean, even a tablet.
Printed on every prescription; 식전 = before meals, 하루 세 번 = three times a day.

items.en: could I have something for a fever
items.note: 진통제 = painkiller, 소화제 = for indigestion, 감기약 = cold medicine.
Adjective + 거 makes 'the ... one': 큰 거, 매운 거, 이거 말고 저거.
덥다 is irregular. 추워요 = I'm cold.
핑크색 is just as common in speech; -색 = colour.
나빠요. For 'it's rubbish' Koreans more often say 별로예요.
길어요. For a tall person say 키가 커요, never 길다.
Blunt and best avoided about people; 통통하다 is the softer 'chubby'.
날씬하다 is the complimentary 'slim'; 말랐어요 can sound like a health worry.
빨라요; 빨리 = quickly, and 빨리빨리 is a national catchphrase.
무거워요.
가벼워요. For a light colour say 연한, for mild food 안 매운.
어느 = which (of a set); 쪽 = side, direction.
한테 = to a person, 한테서 = from a person; 에게(서) is the written form.
랑 is the spoken 'with/and'; 하고 and 와/과 are the neutral and formal versions.
얼마나 걸려요? = how long does it take?
무슨 뜻이에요? asks what a word means.
저의 shrinks to 제, 나의 to 내. Spoken Korean usually drops it: 친구 집 = my friend's place.
저한테 is the polite pair. Choosing 나 or 저 sets your whole register.
그분한테서 is the honorific version.
Contraction of 이것을; likewise 그걸, 저걸, 뭘.
께 replaces 한테 for real deference: 부모님께.
다른 거 = a different one.
아직 안 왔어요 = they haven't come yet.

items.en: the four-way grid: 이거-그거-저거-어느 거, 여기-거기-저기-어디, 이렇게-그렇게-저렇게-어떻게
items.note: 이 = near me, 그 = near you or already mentioned, 저 = away from both of us. The 그 row does the work English 'it' and 'that' do.
역 앞에서 만나요 = let's meet in front of the station.
(으)로 alone also means 'towards': 어디로 가세요?
우리 집, 친구 집; 댁 is the honorific house: 부모님 댁.
보다 is the comparison particle: 이게 저것보다 싸요. 덜 = less.
아니면 = or, or else.
전혀 always needs a negative after it; 별로요 = not really.
The default hedge. Koreans soften opinions with it constantly: 맛있는 것 같아요.
대박 is the everyday 'no way / amazing'.
감사합니다 is the safe default; 고마워요 is warmer and less formal.
The banmal form. Polite is 미안해요, and 죄송합니다 for strangers or anything real.
The discourse opener that buys you a second; 그런데 (그니까/근데) is the other one.
너무 literally 'excessively', but in speech it also just means 'very'.

items.en: the whole lot, all of it
items.note: 다 is the everyday spoken one: 다 먹었어요.
엄청 and 진짜 are the spoken intensifiers; 매우 is textbook-only.

items.en: to become; to work out; to be allowed
items.note: Enormous range: 카드 돼요? (do you take card), 안 돼요 (no can do), 다 됐어요 (all done).
-아/어야 되다 = have to. 가야 해요 is the slightly more formal twin.

items.en: to rest, to have time off
items.note: 오늘 쉬어요 = I'm off today, and also 'we're closed today'.
준비됐어요 = I'm ready / it's ready.
지금 나가요 = I'm heading out now.
금방 올게요 = I'll be right back.

items.en: go in order to do: 밥 먹으러 가요, 보러 왔어요
items.note: Attaches to the verb stem and pairs with 가다/오다/다니다.
Rain 'comes' in Korean. 눈 와요 = it's snowing; 장마 = the summer rainy season.
예약했어요 = I have a booking.
전화 안 받아요 = they're not picking up.
바꾸다 = to swap; the standard 'pass me to' on the phone.
The Uber of Korea, in the 카카오T app; it also books trains and hire bikes.
Signposted in English too; lines are numbered and colour-coded.
기본요금 = the starting fare; the meter always runs, no negotiating.
How you speak to any taxi or bus driver; never 아저씨 to their face.
길이 막혀요 = the roads are jammed; 차 막혀요 in speech.
줄 서세요 = join the queue; 줄이 길어요 = there's a long queue.
걸어서 십 분이요 = ten minutes on foot.
여기서 멀어요? = is it far from here?
연착됐어요 is the announcement word. Korean trains are famously punctual, so you'll use this about buses.
Korean directions are given by numbered subway exit: 6번 출구에서 만나요. The platform itself is 승강장.
-아/어도 돼요? = may I. Careful with 자리 있어요?, which literally asks 'is there a seat?': at a restaurant door it means 'have you got a table free?', so 네 means yes, come in.
지금 가고 있어요 works too.
가격 is the neutral word you see on signs.
현금영수증? = 'cash receipt?' is asked at every till; just say 괜찮아요.
T머니, bought in any convenience store; tap for subway, bus and even taxis. 카카오페이 covers phone payments.
환전 = currency exchange.

items.en: could you do it a bit cheaper
items.note: Only at traditional markets. Shops, cafes and chains have fixed prices and haggling is rude.
깎다 = to shave off. Market-stall only, and best after buying a fair amount.
The spoken default; 휴대폰 is the formal one and 폰 the clip.
Short for 단체 카톡방; where Korean social life is organised.
비디오 now means an old videotape; 영상 통화 = video call.
보조배터리 = power bank.
신호가 안 잡혀요 = there's no reception. 데이터 = mobile data.
어플 is the older spoken form; Korea runs on 네이버 지도 and 카카오맵, not Google Maps.
소리가 안 들려요 = I can't hear you.
통화 = a phone conversation.

items.en: could you put the aircon on

items.note: Young and very spoken. 어머 is the older women's version, 아이고 the all-purpose one.
Works for good news and bad; 진짜? = really?
괜찮아요 does most of the consoling work in Korean.
Hugely frequent: 그냥 왔어요, 그냥 그래요 (I'm just so-so).
-네요 marks something you've just noticed; softer praise than 좋아요.
찾다 covers both looking for and finding.
Korean counts in 만, not thousands: 100,000 is 십만 and 만 원 is the everyday banknote.

items.en: the deep New Year bow to elders
items.note: Done at 설날 in return for 세뱃돈 (money). A normal greeting bow is just 인사.
Temple names end in -사: 불국사. The same word 절 also means a bow.
화났어요 = I'm cross; 짜증 나요 = it's annoying, which you'll hear far more.

items.en: to be scary, to be scared
items.note: 무서워요 covers both the thing and the person.
One verb for both; ㅋㅋㅋ is the written laugh.
바꿔 주세요 = could you change it. 갈아타다 = to change trains.

items.en: that's enough; no thanks; leave it
items.note: Tone does the work: it politely declines an offer and also ends an argument.
노래방 = karaoke room, an inevitable part of a night out.
외로워요. Being alone is 혼자, which is neutral.
The polite way to duck a question or disagree gently; softer than 몰라요.

items.en: take me to this address, please
items.note: Korean taxis always run the meter, so there is nothing to agree in advance. Show the address on your phone and say this.

items.word: 첫 번째, 두 번째, 세 번째…
items.roman: cheot beonjjae, du beonjjae, se beonjjae
items.note: 첫 번째 is irregular (not 한 번째). For dates and floors use Sino numbers instead: 삼 층.
Korean has no 'quarter to' word: 여섯 시 십오 분 전, or just say 다섯 시 사십오 분.
횡단보도 = the pedestrian crossing; jaywalking is genuinely fined.
Dial 119 for ambulance and fire, 112 for police.
주문할게요 = I'd like to order. In speech 시키다 is common: 뭐 시킬까요?
저기서 오른쪽으로 도세요. Signs use 우회전 (right turn) and 좌회전 (left turn).
Korean relative clauses go in front of the noun: 밥 먹는 곳 = a place to eat.

items.en: nothing to be done about it
items.note: The resigned shrug; 할 수 없죠 works the same.
Signs and manuals. In speech use 쓰다.
공 is what you say in phone numbers: 공일공 = 010.
Money is spoken in 만 units: 15,000 won is 만 오천 원.
주말 잘 보내세요 = have a good weekend; 평일 = weekdays.

items.en: dates: Sino number + 월, Sino number + 일
items.note: Big to small, year then month then day. Watch 유월 (not 육월) and 시월 (not 십월).
Korean months are simply number + 월, so all twelve cost you one rule.
Irregular: 육월 is wrong.
Irregular: 십월 is wrong.
Very common in men's speech; 아내 is the neutral word and 집사람 the old-fashioned one.
상견례, the two families' first meeting, matters more socially.
Also used jokingly for 'my husband'. 신부 = bride.
The respectful term of address; seats on the subway are reserved for 어르신.
Blunt about a person. Say 나이가 많으세요 or 연세가 있으세요 instead.
뼈해장국 is a well-known pork-bone soup.
써요. Same spelling as 쓰다 'to use' and 'to write'; context separates them.
먹어 보다 (try eating) is the everyday way to say it.
Markets sell meat and veg by the 근; shops use kilos and grams.
인덕션 = induction hob, now common in new flats.
봉투 (carrier bag) is chargeable at every shop, so bring your own.
Everyone carries one in the Korean summer; 부채 is the folding paper fan.
Runs the underfloor heating (온돌) as well as the taps.
땀 나요 = I'm sweating.
등산 (hill walking) is the national hobby; 내려가다 = to go down.
Said to elders in the morning; 잘 잤어요? between equals. 좋은 아침 is a translation nobody really uses.
안녕히 주무세요 to anyone older; 잘 자 in banmal.
A host's offer. Staff say 뭐 드릴까요? or 주문하시겠어요?
오랜만이야 in banmal; 잘 지냈어요? usually follows.
신경 쓰지 마세요 = don't give it a thought. -지 마세요 = please don't.
Literally 'I want to see you', and it also means exactly that.
바빠요. 요즘 바빠요? is standard small talk.
한가해요 is the adjective; 시간 있어요? = are you free?
Asked as 무슨 일 하세요?, not 직업이 뭐예요? which sounds like a form.
한국어 공부해요 = I'm learning Korean. 공부 is a verb-noun with 하다.
대학생 = a student. Many subway stations are named after one.
A safe and welcome conversation topic; 예능 = variety shows.
야구 fills the stadiums; 축구 is what you'll be asked about, usually with 손흥민 in the same breath.
소식 = news of a person: 소식 들었어요?
병원 covers hospital and clinic alike, so 응급실 is the A&E department inside it. Dial 119 for an ambulance, 112 for police.
무릎이 아파요, a stock complaint after all that hill walking.
이거 좀 잡아 주세요 = hold this a sec; 택시 잡다 = to catch a taxi.
Of things. A person falling over is 넘어지다.
Pour with two hands for anyone older, and never top up your own glass.
아무나 (anyone), 아무거나 (anything, the standard answer to 뭐 먹을까요?), 아무도 + negative (nobody).
Both future and guess: 집에 있을 거예요 = they'll be at home / they're probably at home.

items.en: about to, intending to: 나가려고 해요
items.note: For 'just this second about to', use 막 나가려던 참이에요.
제대로 안 됐어요 = it hasn't been done properly. 잘 = well.

items.en: stay and eat before you go
items.note: The classic Korean host line, and often just a warm goodbye rather than a literal offer.

items.en: let me know when you get there
items.note: 연락 주세요 = get in touch; -(으)면 = when/if.
잘한다 to a child. To praise an adult's work, 수고하셨어요 is safer.
귀여워요, and it is used constantly: babies, pets, objects, grown adults.
Shoes come off at the door of homes, many guesthouses and some restaurants; 실내화 = indoor shoes.
The other big one is 설날 (lunar new year). Both empty the cities and fill the motorways.
Said 'yeo-kkwon'. Needed for tax-free shopping and any sim card.
이거 써도 돼요? = can I use this? Also means 'to write'. 사용하다 is the formal twin.
Korean couples also count in days: 100일, 1000일.
안경 쓰다 = to wear glasses, the same 쓰다 again.

items.en: word order: the verb always lands last
items.note: Korean is subject-object-verb, and the particles (은/는, 이/가, 을/를) do the job English does with position. Anything obvious is simply dropped: 어디 가요?, 먹었어요?

items.word: 덥다 → 더워요 / 듣다 → 들어요 / 모르다 → 몰라요
items.roman: deopda → deowoyo / deutda → deureoyo / moreuda → mollayo
items.en: irregular stems: the verbs that change shape before 아/어요
items.note: ㅂ→우 (맵다 매워요, 춥다 추워요), ㄷ→ㄹ (걷다 걸어요), ㅡ drops (바쁘다 바빠요, 쓰다 써요), 르→ㄹㄹ (빠르다 빨라요), ㅅ drops (낫다 나아요). Five patterns cover nearly every verb you meet.
갈게요 'right, I'm off', 이걸로 할게요 'I'll take this one', 계산할게요 'I'll pay'. Only ever about yourself, and only as a response to the other person; a plain plan is -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

items.en: …, isn't it – reacting to what's in front of you
items.note: 맛있네요, 비싸네요, 한국말 잘하시네요. Marks something you have just noticed, and it is how compliments and small talk are actually made: 날씨 좋네요.

items.en: the 합니다 level: 갑니다, 먹습니다, 감사합니다
items.note: Vowel stem + ㅂ니다 (갑니다), consonant stem + 습니다 (먹습니다); questions take -ㅂ니까?/-습니까?. Mostly a recognition skill – staff, announcements and the news aim it at you all day.

items.en: the long negative: 가지 않아요 = I don't go
items.note: Same meaning as 안 가요, but commoner in writing and careful speech. 맛없다 and 재미없다 are their own words, not built with this.

items.en: to get on; to ride; to take (transport)
items.note: 타요. 버스 타고 가요, 택시 탈까요?, 몇 번 버스 타요? The pair is 내리다, and you tap your card getting on and off.
갈아타요. 2호선으로 갈아타세요. The sign and announcement word is 환승, which is also what the card reader says at you.
건너요. 길 건너세요, 횡단보도 건너서 왼쪽이요. Jaywalking is genuinely fined, so wait for the green man.
Sino numbers: 삼 층, 몇 층이에요?, 지하 일 층 for the basement. Korean bars and restaurants stack up buildings, so the floor is part of the address.
GS25, CU, 세븐일레븐 – open all night on every corner, and where you top up a 교통카드, get hot food and find a cash machine.
The everyday word for anywhere serving a meal; 카페 for coffee, 술집 for drinks. 맛집 = a place worth going out of your way for.
체크아웃 몇 시예요? 'what time is checkout?'. Nights are counted with 박: 이 박 삼 일 = two nights, three days.
영수증 주세요, or 괜찮아요 to wave it away. The other till question is 봉투 필요하세요? 'do you want a bag?', and bags are chargeable.
The first thing a café or fast-food till asks. Answer 여기서 먹을게요 or 포장이요.
따뜻해요. The café question is 따뜻한 거요, 아이스요?; 뜨겁다 is scalding, 시원하다 is pleasantly cool and is also said of soup and beer.
The default Korean coffee, iced all year round: 아이스 아메리카노, clipped to 아아. 따아 is the hot one; 라떼 is the other staple.
생맥주 draught, 병맥주 bottled, 소맥 the soju-and-beer mix. 맥주 한 잔 더 주세요.
건배! or 위하여!. Hold your glass lower than an elder's, turn away for the first sip, and never fill your own.
Native numbers: 스무 살, 서른두 살, 마흔 살. Age decides who may speak banmal to whom, so it comes up in the first minute of a conversation.
Normal between peers and not rude in Korean. To anyone older say 나이가 어떻게 되세요?, and 연세가 어떻게 되세요? to an elderly person.
미세먼지 심해요 'the air's bad today'. Checked on the phone like the forecast, and the stock spring complaint.

items.en: thanks for your trouble; well done
items.note: Said to anyone who has just done a job for you, and between colleagues at the end of the day. To someone clearly senior, 고생 많으셨습니다 or plain 감사합니다 is safer.

items.en: I look forward to it; please be good to me
items.note: Closes any first introduction, straight after 만나서 반갑습니다. There is no English equivalent; it is simply what you say.
Opens a question to a stranger: 실례지만 여기가 어디예요? 저기요 gets their attention first; 실례합니다 is for squeezing past.
백 원, 이백, 팔백. Prices are read from the top down: 15,500 is 만 오천오백 원.
Called out by every shop, café and restaurant as you walk in. Nothing is expected back; a nod is plenty.
Said at the till on the way out, which is where you pay in Korea. 따로 계산해 주세요 = separately, 같이 계산할게요 = all together.

items.en: right, tucking in / that was lovely, thank you
items.note: Said before and after any meal someone else has cooked or paid for. The 합니다 form is standard here even among friends.
The first thing said to a British visitor, usually with 손흥민 and 토트넘 attached. 야구 fills the stadiums; 경기 = a match.
Korea does all four hard: 벚꽃 blossom in spring, 장마 rains in summer, 단풍 autumn colour, and a Seoul winter well below freezing.

items.en: this stop is …, doors open on the right
items.note: The subway announcement, in 합니다 style and repeated in English after the Korean. 다음 역 = the next stop, 환승 = change here.

items.en: have you got an English menu?
items.note: Outside tourist areas menus are Korean-only with no pictures. 사진 있어요? 'any photos?' is the fallback, and pointing at the next table works too.
